danish.title: Sjette bog (1808–10) — Kapitel 13
paragraphs: En aften, da den gamle grevinde i natkappe og natkjole, uden sine falske krøller og med sin stakkels lille hårknold synlig under den hvide bomuldskappe, knælede sukkende og stønnende på et tæppe og bøjede sig til jorden i bøn, knirkede døren, og Natasja, også i natkjole med tøfler på bare fødder og håret i papillotter, løb ind. Grevinden — med sin andægtige stemning forstyrret — vendte sig om og rynkede panden. Hun var ved at afslutte sin sidste bøn: »Kan det mon være, at denne seng bliver min grav?« Natasja, rødmende og ivrig, og da hun så sin mor i bøn, standsede brat, satte sig halvt ned og stak uvilkårligt tunge af sig selv, som for at skælde sig ud. Da hun så, at moderen stadig bad, løb hun på tåspidserne hen til sengen og gled hurtigt den ene lille fod mod den anden, sparkede tøflerne af og hoppede op i sengen, som grevinden havde frygtet ville blive hendes grav. Denne seng var høj med en dyne og fem puder, den ene mindre end den under. Natasja hoppede op i den, sank ned i dynen, rullede hen til væggen og begyndte at putte sig ind under tæpperne, idet hun trak knæene op under hagen, sparkede ud og lo næsten uhørligt, snart gemte sig helt med tæppet over hovedet og snart kiggede frem mod sin mor. Grevinden afsluttede sine bønner og kom hen til sengen med et strengt ansigt, men da hun så, at Natasjas hoved var tildækket, smilede hun på sin venlige, svage måde.
»Nå, nå!« sagde hun.

»Mamma, kan vi ikke tale lidt? Ja?« sagde Natasja. »Se, bare ét kys her på halsen og endnu ét... sådan!« Og hun greb sin mor om halsen og kyssede hende på struben. I sin opførsel over for moderen virkede Natasja barsk, men hun var så følsom og taktfuld, at uanset hvordan hun omfavnede hende, formåede hun altid at gøre det uden at gøre hende ondt eller bringe hende i forlegenhed.

»Nå, hvad er der i aften?« sagde moderen, da hun havde ordnet sine puder og ventet, til Natasja, efter at have vendt sig et par gange, havde lagt sig til rette ved siden af hende under dynen, bredt armene ud og antaget et alvorligt udtryk.
Disse natlige besøg af Natasja, inden greven kom hjem fra sin klub, var en af de største glæder for både mor og datter.
»Hvad er der i aften? — Men jeg har noget at fortælle dig...«
Natasja lagde sin hånd over moderens mund.
»Om Boris... det ved jeg,« sagde hun alvorligt, »det er det, jeg er kommet for at tale om. Sig det ikke — jeg ved det. Nej, fortæl alligevel!« Og hun fjernede hånden. »Sig mig, mamma! Er han sød?«

»Natasja, du er seksten. I din alder var jeg gift. Du siger, Boris er sød. Han er meget sød, og jeg elsker ham som en søn. Men hvad så?... Hvad tænker du på? Du har fuldstændig fordreje hovedet på ham, det kan jeg se...«

Idet hun sagde dette, vendte grevinden sig mod sin datter. Natasja lå og stirrede stift lige frem mod en af de mahogni-sfinkser, der var udskåret på sengehjørnerne, så grevinden kun så sin datters ansigt i profil. Det ansigt slog hende ved sit særligt alvorlige og koncentrerede udtryk.
Natasja lyttede og overvejede.
»Nå, hvad så?« sagde hun.
»Du har fuldstændigt fordrejet hovedet på ham, og hvorfor? Hvad vil du med ham? Du ved, du ikke kan gifte dig med ham.«
»Hvorfor ikke?« sagde Natasja uden at ændre stilling.
»Fordi han er ung, fordi han er fattig, fordi han er i familie med os... og fordi du ikke elsker ham selv.«
»Hvordan ved du det?«
»Det ved jeg bare. Det er ikke rigtigt, min skat!«
»Men hvis nu jeg vil...« sagde Natasja.
»Hold op med det vrøvl,« sagde grevinden.
»Men hvis nu jeg vil...«
»Natasja, nu mener jeg det alvorligt...«

Natasja lod hende ikke tale ud. Hun trak grevindens store hånd til sig, kyssede den på bagsiden og derefter på håndfladen, vendte den om igen og begyndte at kysse først den ene kno, så mellemrummet mellem knoerne, så den næste, mens hun hviskede: »Januar, februar, marts, april, maj. Tal, mamma, hvorfor siger du ikke noget? Tal!« sagde hun og vendte sig mod sin mor, der ømt betragtede sin datter og i den betragten syntes at have glemt alt, hvad hun havde villet sige.

»Det går ikke an, min skat! Ikke alle vil forstå dette venskab fra jeres barndom, og at se ham så fortrolig med dig kan skade dig i øjnene på andre unge mænd, der besøger os, og frem for alt plager det ham for ingenting. Han har måske allerede fundet et passende og velhavende parti, og nu er han halvt fra forstanden.«
»Fra forstanden?« gentog Natasja.
»Jeg skal fortælle dig noget om mig selv. Jeg havde en fætter...«
»Det ved jeg! Kirill Matveïtj... men han er gammel.«
»Det var han ikke altid. Men her er, hvad jeg vil gøre, Natasja: jeg taler med Boris. Han behøver ikke komme så tit...«
»Hvorfor ikke, hvis han kan lide det?«
»Fordi jeg ved, det ender med ingenting...«

»Hvordan kan du vide det? Nej, mamma, tal ikke med ham! Sikke noget vrøvl!« sagde Natasja i tonen fra en, der bliver berøvet sin ejendom. »Nå, jeg gifter mig ikke, men lad ham komme, hvis han nyder det, og jeg nyder det.« Natasja smilede og så på sin mor. »Ikke for at gifte mig, men bare... sådan,« tilføjede hun.
»Hvordan sådan, min skat?«
»Bare sådan. Der er ikke behov for, at jeg gifter mig med ham. Men... bare sådan.«
»Bare sådan, bare sådan,« gentog grevinden og gik rystende over hele kroppen i en godmodig, uventet, gammelkvindeagtig latter.

»Lad være med at le, hold op!« råbte Natasja. »Du ryster hele sengen! Du ligner forfærdeligt mig, sådan en fniser du også er... Vent...« Og hun greb grevindens hænder og kyssede en kno på lillefingeren og sagde: »Juni,« og fortsatte med at kysse: »Juli, august,« på den anden hånd. »Men mamma, er han meget forelsket? Hvad tror du? Har nogen nogensinde været så forelsket i dig? Og han er meget sød, rigtig, rigtig sød. Bare ikke helt min smag — han er så smal, som spisesal-uret... Kan du ikke forstå? Smal, ved du — grå, lysegrå...«
»Sikke noget vrøvl du snakker!« sagde grevinden.
Natasja fortsatte: »Kan du virkelig ikke forstå? Nikolaj ville forstå det... Bezukhov, derimod, er blå, mørkeblå og rød, og han er firkantet.«
»Du flirter med ham også,« sagde grevinden leende.
»Nej, han er frimurer, det har jeg fundet ud af. Han er fin, mørkeblå og rød... Hvordan skal jeg forklare det for dig?«
»Lille grevinde!« lød grevens stemme bag døren. »Er du ikke faldet i søvn?« Natasja sprang op, rev sine tøfler til sig og løb barfodet til sit eget værelse.
Der gik lang tid, før hun kunne falde i søvn. Hun blev ved med at tænke, at ingen kunne forstå alt det, hun forstod, og alt det, der var i hende.

»Sonja?« tænkte hun og skottede til den sammenrullede, sovende lille killing med sin enorme hårfletning. »Nej, hvordan skulle hun kunne? Hun er dydig. Hun blev forelsket i Nikolaj og ønsker ikke at vide mere. Selv mamma forstår det ikke. Det er vidunderligt, hvor klog jeg er, og hvor... charmerende hun er,« fortsatte hun og talte om sig selv i tredje person, idet hun forestillede sig, at det var en meget klog mand — den viseste og bedste af mænd — der sagde det om hende. »Der er alt, alt i hende,« fortsatte denne mand. »Hun er usædvanlig intelligent, charmerende... og så er hun smuk, usædvanlig smuk, og adræt — hun svømmer og rider glimrende... og hendes stemme! Man kan virkelig sige, det er en vidunderlig stemme!«

Hun nynnede et stykke fra sin yndlingsopera af Cherubini, kastede sig på sengen, lo over den behagelige tanke, at hun straks ville falde i søvn, kaldte på stuepigen Dunjasja for at slukke lyset, og inden Dunjasja havde forladt rummet, var hun allerede gledet ind i endnu en lykkeligere drømmeverden, hvor alting var lige så lyst og smukt som i virkeligheden og endnu smukkere, fordi det var anderledes.
Næste dag kaldte grevinden Boris til side og havde en samtale med ham, hvorefter han holdt op med at komme hos Rostoverne.

english.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: One night when the old countess, in her nightcap and dressing jacket, without her false curls and with her thin little knob of hair showing under a white cotton cap, was kneeling on a rug, sighing and groaning as she bowed to the ground in prayer, her door creaked and Natasha — also in a dressing jacket, with slippers on her bare feet and her hair in curlers — ran in. The countess, her prayerful mood shattered, looked around and frowned. She was just finishing her last prayer: "Can it be that this bed will be my grave?" Natasha, flushed and eager, seeing her mother at prayer, suddenly checked her rush, half sat down, and unconsciously stuck out her tongue as if scolding herself. Seeing that her mother was still praying, she tiptoed to the bed and, quickly slipping one bare foot against the other, kicked off her slippers and jumped onto the bed the countess had feared might become her grave. This bed was high, with a feather mattress and five pillows, each smaller than the one below. Natasha jumped onto it, sank into the feather mattress, rolled over toward the wall, and began snuggling under the covers as she settled in, pulling her knees up to her chin, kicking out and laughing almost silently — now burying herself head and all, now peeking out at her mother. The countess finished her prayers and came to the bed with a stern face, but seeing that Natasha's head was covered, she smiled in her kind, gentle way.
"Now then, now then!" she said.

"Mama, can we talk? Yes?" said Natasha. "Now, just one kiss on your neck and another... that'll do!" And seizing her mother around the neck, she kissed her on the throat. In her behavior toward her mother Natasha seemed rough, but she was so sensitive and tactful that however she grabbed her mother she always managed to do it without hurting her or making her uncomfortable.

"Well, what is it tonight?" said the mother, having arranged her pillows and waited until Natasha, after turning over a couple of times, had settled down beside her under the quilt, spread out her arms, and put on a serious expression.
These nighttime visits of Natasha's, before the count returned from his club, were one of the greatest pleasures of both mother and daughter.
"What is it tonight? — But I have to tell you..."
Natasha put her hand over her mother's mouth.
"About Boris... I know," she said seriously, "that's what I've come about. Don't say it — I know. No, do tell me!" and she removed her hand. "Tell me, Mama! Is he nice?"

"Natasha, you are sixteen. At your age I was married. You say Boris is nice. He is very nice, and I love him like a son. But what then?... What are you thinking about? You've completely turned his head, I can see that..."

As she said this the countess looked around at her daughter. Natasha was lying gazing steadily straight ahead at one of the mahogany sphinxes carved on the corners of the bedstead, so that the countess could only see her daughter's face in profile. That face struck her by its peculiarly serious and concentrated expression.
Natasha was listening and thinking.
"Well, what then?" said she.
"You've completely turned his head, and why? What do you want from him? You know you can't marry him."
"Why not?" said Natasha, without changing her position.
"Because he's young, because he's poor, because he's a relative... and because you yourself don't love him."
"How do you know?"
"I know. It's not right, darling!"
"But if I want to..." said Natasha.
"Stop talking nonsense," said the countess.
"But if I want to..."
"Natasha, I am serious..."

Natasha didn't let her finish. She took the countess's large hand, kissed it on the back, then on the palm, then turned it over and began kissing first one knuckle, then the space between knuckles, then the next knuckle, whispering: "January, February, March, April, May. Say something, Mama — why are you quiet? Say something!" she cried, turning to her mother, who was gazing tenderly at her daughter and in that contemplation seemed to have forgotten everything she had meant to say.

"It won't do, my love! Not everyone will understand this friendship dating from your childhood, and seeing him so close to you may harm you in the eyes of other young men who visit us, and above all it torments him for nothing. He may already have found a suitable and wealthy match, and now he's half out of his mind."
"Half out of his mind?" repeated Natasha.
"Let me tell you something about myself. I had a cousin..."
"I know! Kirill Matveich... but he's old."
"He wasn't always old. But here's what I'll do, Natasha — I'll have a talk with Boris. He needn't come so often..."
"Why not, if he wants to?"
"Because I know it will come to nothing..."

"How can you know? No, Mama, don't talk to him! What nonsense!" said Natasha in the tone of someone being robbed of her property. "Well, I won't marry him, but let him come if he enjoys it and I enjoy it." Natasha smiled and looked at her mother. "Not to get married, but just... just so," she added.
"How so, my pet?"
"Just so. There's no need to marry him. But... just so."
"Just so, just so," repeated the countess, and shaking all over, she burst into a good-natured, unexpected, elderly laugh.

"Don't laugh, stop!" cried Natasha. "You're shaking the whole bed! You're terribly like me, just the same kind of giggler... Wait..." and she seized the countess's hands and kissed a knuckle on the little finger, saying, "June," and continued, kissing, "July, August," on the other hand. "But, Mama, is he very much in love? What do you think? Was anybody ever so much in love with you? And he's very nice, very, very nice. Only not quite my type — he's so narrow, like the dining room clock... Don't you understand? Narrow, you know — gray, light gray..."
"What rubbish you're talking!" said the countess.
Natasha continued: "Don't you really understand? Nicholas would understand... Bezukhov, now — he's blue, dark blue and red, and he's square."
"You flirt with him too," said the countess, laughing.
"No, he's a Freemason, I've figured it out. He's fine — dark blue and red... How can I explain it to you?"
"Little countess!" the count's voice called from behind the door. "You're not asleep?" Natasha jumped up, snatched her slippers, and ran barefoot to her own room.
It was a long time before she could fall asleep. She kept thinking that no one could understand everything she understood and everything there was inside her.

"Sonya?" she thought, glancing at the curled-up, sleeping little kitten with her enormous braid of hair. "No, how could she? She's so virtuous. She fell in love with Nicholas and doesn't want to know anything more. Even Mama doesn't understand. It's amazing how clever I am and how... charming she is," she went on, speaking of herself in the third person, imagining it was some very wise man — the wisest and best of men — saying it about her. "She has everything, everything," this man continued. "She is unusually intelligent, charming... and then she is pretty, extraordinarily pretty, and agile — she swims and rides superbly... and her voice! One can honestly say it's a wonderful voice!"

She hummed a snippet from her favorite opera by Cherubini, threw herself on her bed, laughed at the pleasant thought that she would fall asleep immediately, called Dunyasha the maid to blow out the candle, and before Dunyasha had even left the room she had already drifted into another, happier world of dreams, where everything was as light and beautiful as in reality, and even more so because it was different.
The next day the countess called Boris aside and had a talk with him, after which he stopped coming to the Rostovs'.
